body:
## Resolution
Category: correctness. Area: manage.sh (`require_running_container`, `run_lgsm`, `run_lgsm_noninteractive`, `show_status_one`, `show_logs`, `open_shell`, `exec_in_container`). Every command routed through `for_target()` calls its callback as `"$callback" "$service" "$@" || failed=1`. Per documented bash semantics, a shell function invoked as the tested command of an `||` list has `set -e` ignored for every command it executes, transitively. The 7 internal `id=$(require_container ...)` / `id=$(require_running_container ...)` assignments were unguarded, so when `die()` fired (only exiting its own command-substitution subshell) the failure was silently discarded and execution continued with an empty `id`, ultimately reaching `docker exec`/`docker inspect` with an empty container ID. Reproduced with a mock `docker` binary: `restart all` with Valheim's container missing printed both correct diagnostics, then a misleading "proceeding" log line (`./vhserver restart ()`), then a raw `Error: No such container:` from the exec call — the script's own guard clauses did not stop it; only Docker's own input validation did.
Fix applied: added `|| return 1` after each of the 7 unguarded lookups (explicit `return` is not subject to the `-e` exemption). Re-verified: `restart all` with Valheim missing now prints exactly one clean diagnostic for Valheim and correctly continues to restart the remaining servers (exit code 1, correctly reflecting the partial failure); `restart valheim` alone now stops cleanly after exactly one diagnostic.

Migrated from v1 `nitpicker-findings.md` (Pass 1, 2026-07-30).
title: `die()` does not abort bulk/per-target operations; script silently proceeds with an empty container ID

body:
## Resolution
Category: conventions. Area: manage.sh (`DISPLAY_NAMES`, `DEFAULT_SCRIPTS`). shellcheck 0.11.0 does not parse keys in a `readonly -A NAME=(...)` literal as associative-array string keys the way it does for `declare -A`, instead treating hyphenated keys as arithmetic subtraction of bare words, producing 8 SC2154 warnings. Confirmed via isolated repro that splitting into `declare -A NAME=(...)` + separate `readonly NAME` eliminates all warnings with identical runtime behavior.
Fix applied: replaced both `readonly -A NAME=(...)` declarations with `declare -A NAME=(...)` followed by `readonly NAME`. `shellcheck manage.sh` now exits 0 with no warnings.

Migrated from v1 `nitpicker-findings.md` (Pass 1, 2026-07-30).
title: `readonly -A` associative-array declarations trigger 8 shellcheck SC2154 false positives

body:
## Problem

`upgrade_one()` calls `run_lgsm_noninteractive "$service" update-lgsm`, then `update`, then `validate` as three unguarded sequential statements with no `||`/return-status check between them. `upgrade_one` is invoked as `"$callback" "$service" "$@" || failed=1` inside `for_target()` (same pattern documented in the now-fixed finding for require_container/require_running_container): a shell function called as the tested command of an `||` list has `-e` ignored for everything it executes, so a failing first or second step does not stop the third from running.

## Evidence

Reproduced with a mock `docker` binary: `./manage.sh upgrade valheim` with Valheim's container missing prints the identical diagnostic three times —
```
[ERR ] No Coolify-managed container found for 'valheim'. Deploy docker-compose.yaml first.
[ERR ] No Coolify-managed container found for 'valheim'. Deploy docker-compose.yaml first.
[ERR ] No Coolify-managed container found for 'valheim'. Deploy docker-compose.yaml first.
```
(exit=1). The now-fixed `require_running_container` guard stops each individual `run_lgsm_noninteractive` call cleanly, but `upgrade_one` itself has no equivalent guard between its three steps, so all three run and each independently hits and reports the same failure.

## Impact

Cosmetic in the missing-container case (tripled, redundant diagnostic instead of one). More significant when the container is running but `update-lgsm` fails for a real reason (network error, upstream LinuxGSM issue): `upgrade_one` proceeds to run `update` and then `validate` against a LinuxGSM installation that may be in a partially-updated, inconsistent state from the failed `update-lgsm` step, contradicting the documented sequential dependency ("`upgrade` runs these LinuxGSM operations sequentially") and risking a misleading "validate: OK" result over broken state.

## Fix

Add `|| return 1` after each of the three calls in `upgrade_one`:
```bash
upgrade_one() {
  local service=$1
  run_lgsm_noninteractive "$service" update-lgsm || return 1
  run_lgsm_noninteractive "$service" update || return 1
  run_lgsm_noninteractive "$service" validate || return 1
}
```

## Resolution
Added `|| return 1` after each of the 3 sequential calls in upgrade_one(). Verified: bats regression test "upgrade stops after the first failed step instead of repeating the diagnostic" fails on the pre-fix code (diagnostic printed 3x) and passes post-fix (printed once); "upgrade all skips the missing service but still upgrades the rest" confirms the remaining targets still complete.
title: upgrade_one() doesn't stop after a failed step, so update/validate run even after update-lgsm fails

body:
## Problem

All four services reference `ghcr.io/gameservermanagers/gameserver:<shortname>` (`:mc`, `:pz`, `:vh`, `:sdtd`) by mutable tag. The upstream image's own README states "This container image builds weekly," meaning the content behind each tag changes on a schedule without a corresponding version bump in this repo.

## Evidence

docker-compose.yaml lines 3, 19, 35, 51 all use bare `:<shortname>` tags with no digest. Confirmed via the upstream `GameServerManagers/docker-gameserver` README that the image "builds weekly."

## Impact

Every redeploy (Coolify re-pull, host reboot that re-pulls, etc.) can silently pull a different image build than the last deploy. A breaking change in a weekly upstream build affects all four servers simultaneously with no way to correlate the break to a repo change, and there is no way to redeploy an exact previously-known-good image state.

## Fix

Pin each image to a digest (`image: ghcr.io/gameservermanagers/gameserver:mc@sha256:...`) and update the digest deliberately (e.g. via a periodic manual bump or a Renovate/Dependabot digest-update rule), or at minimum document in README that redeploys are not reproducible and how to roll back to a prior digest via the registry.

## Resolution
Resolved each tag's current manifest digest from the GHCR registry API (anonymous pull token + Docker-Content-Digest header) and pinned all 4 images to tag@digest. Verified all 4 digests are well-formed (64 hex chars) and that `docker compose config` resolves each image reference to the exact intended string with no inserted whitespace. Wrapped the resulting long lines using YAML double-quoted backslash line-continuation (verified via `docker compose config` that this introduces zero extra characters) to keep yamllint's line-length rule clean.
title: Game server images are pinned to floating tags, not digests, for images that build weekly

body:
## Problem

manage.sh is a 440-line bash script with meaningful branching logic (command dispatch, per-target iteration, container lookup with multiple failure modes) and zero automated tests. There is no bats/shunit2 harness, and nothing exercises the failure paths (missing container, stopped container, multi-step command sequences).

## Evidence

`find . -type f` shows no `*.bats`, `test/`, or `tests/` directory. This exact untested surface already harbored two confirmed correctness bugs found this session purely by manual reasoning plus ad hoc mock-`docker` testing: the `for_target`/`die()` error-propagation bug (now fixed) and `upgrade_one()`'s un-guarded three-step sequence (filed separately) — both are exactly the class of bug a small scripted test with a stub `docker` binary would catch mechanically and keep catching on future changes.

## Impact

Regressions in the container-lookup/error-handling logic (the part of the script proven fragile) can be reintroduced silently by any future edit, with no automated signal before a real deployment surfaces it.

## Fix

Add a small `bats-core` (or `shunit2`) test suite under `test/` that stubs `docker` via `PATH` injection (the same technique used to verify this session's fixes) and covers: missing container, stopped container, and the multi-step `upgrade` sequence for both single-target and `all`.

## Resolution
Added test/manage.bats (bats-core), stubbing `docker` via PATH injection. 8 tests covering: missing-container error propagation (single-target and `all`), the upgrade-sequence short-circuit, `list`'s non-fatal missing-container reporting, and unknown-server/command rejection. Verified the suite is not tautological: the two regression-focused tests fail against a copy of the code with the NP-001/upgrade_one fixes reverted, and pass against the current fixed code.
title: No automated tests exist for manage.sh's command dispatch and error-propagation logic

body:
## Problem

`manage.sh monitor <server|all>` runs "LinuxGSM monitor check" (a process-responsiveness check LinuxGSM can use to detect and restart a hung-but-still-running game server), but nothing in the repository invokes it periodically. Docker's `restart: unless-stopped` policy only recovers a container that has actually exited; it cannot detect a game process that is alive but unresponsive.

## Evidence

`manage.sh` implements and documents `monitor` (usage text, README "Commands" table) but the repository contains no cron file, systemd timer, or Coolify scheduled-task config that calls it, and README's "Management" section only shows it as a manually-typed example command.

## Impact

A hung (not crashed) game server process is not auto-recovered — only a container restart, not a hung process, is covered by the existing restart policy. Recovery depends entirely on an operator remembering to run `./manage.sh monitor all` by hand.

## Fix

Document (or provide) a periodic invocation, e.g. a host crontab entry (`*/5 * * * * /path/to/manage.sh monitor all`) or a Coolify scheduled task, and mention it in README's "Management" section.

## Resolution
Added a crontab example and explanation to README.md's "Management" section, documenting why `monitor` needs external scheduling (Docker's restart policy only recovers exited containers, not hung-but-alive processes).
title: LinuxGSM's `monitor` self-healing command is implemented but never scheduled to run automatically

body:
## Problem

The repository has no `LICENSE` (or `LICENSE.md`/`COPYING`) file declaring the terms under which this code may be used, copied, or modified.

## Evidence

`find . -type f -not -path './.git/*'` lists `docker-compose.yaml`, `manage.sh`, `README.md`, `.env.example`, and `docs/audit/findings/*` — no license file anywhere.

## Impact

Without an explicit license, the default legal position in most jurisdictions (and GitHub's own stated policy) is that no one else has any right to use, copy, or modify the code, even if the repository itself is publicly visible. This is inconsistent with a repo polished enough to document deployment and management for other Coolify/LinuxGSM users.

## Fix

Add a `LICENSE` file with the owner's chosen license (e.g. MIT, Apache-2.0) and, if desired, reference it from README.md.

## Resolution
Added LICENSE (MIT, user's choice) and a short "License" section in README.md linking to it.
title: No LICENSE file in the repository

body:
## Problem

`mem_limit: ${MINECRAFT_MEMORY_LIMIT:-8g}` sizes the *container*, but the
Minecraft server is a JVM whose usable memory is bounded by `-Xmx`, not by the
cgroup limit. LinuxGSM's `mcserver` ships `javaram="1024"`, and nothing in this
repo overrides it. The server therefore runs with a 1 GB max heap inside an
8 GiB container: ~7 GB of the limit is permanently unreachable, and the server
hits `java.lang.OutOfMemoryError` long before the container limit is relevant.

Meanwhile `server.properties` advertises `max-players=20`.

## Evidence

Live container on this host (`ghcr.io/gameservermanagers/gameserver:mc`, up 16h):

```
$ docker exec <mc> ps -eo args | grep java
sh -c java -Xmx1024M -jar ./minecraft_server.jar nogui

$ docker inspect --format '{{.HostConfig.Memory}}' <mc>
8589934592          # 8 GiB

$ docker stats --no-stream
minecraft   487.6MiB / 8GiB   5.95%

$ docker exec <mc> grep max-players /data/serverfiles/server.properties
max-players=20
```

Upstream source of the cap, `lgsm/config-default/config-lgsm/mcserver/_default.cfg`:

```
12:  javaram="1024" # -Xmx$1024M
174: preexecutable="java -Xmx${javaram}M -jar"
```

Documented sizing for a 10-player vanilla server is 4-8 GB of heap
(minecraft.fandom.com `Server/Requirements/Dedicated`; hosting guidance
converges on 6-8 GB for 10 players). 1 GB is below every published figure - it
is roughly the documented figure for 1-2 players.

## Impact

With 10 concurrent players the JVM heap exhausts: first sustained full-GC pauses
(multi-second tick freezes, "Can't keep up! Is the server overloaded?"), then
`OutOfMemoryError` and server death. Because the JVM dies rather than the
container, Docker's `restart: unless-stopped` does NOT recover it - the
container stays up with a dead game process, and LinuxGSM `monitor` is the only
thing that would notice. Raising `MINECRAFT_MEMORY_LIMIT` has no effect
whatsoever; the operator-facing knob this repo documents is inert for this
service.

## Fix

Set `javaram` in the instance config that already exists in the named volume
(`/data/config-lgsm/mcserver/mcserver.cfg`), sizing heap below the container
limit so JVM non-heap memory (metaspace, code cache, thread stacks, GC
structures) fits inside `mem_limit`:

```bash
./manage.sh exec minecraft sh -lc \
  'echo "javaram=\"6144\"" >> /data/config-lgsm/mcserver/mcserver.cfg'
./manage.sh restart minecraft
```

6144 MB heap inside the 8 GiB limit leaves ~2 GB for JVM overhead. Document the
knob in `.env.example`/README so it is not silently lost: `*_MEMORY_LIMIT` must
be described as "container limit - must exceed the game's own heap setting", and
the Minecraft heap must be called out as separately configured.

## Resolution
Set javaram="6144" in /data/config-lgsm/mcserver/mcserver.cfg and restarted. Verified live: process is now 'java -Xmx6144M -jar ./minecraft_server.jar nogui' (was -Xmx1024M). Container listening on 25565 tcp/udp. README now documents javaram as the effective Minecraft memory knob.
title: Minecraft JVM heap is capped at 1 GB by LinuxGSM, so the 8g mem_limit is unreachable and 10 players cannot be served

body:
## Problem

Project Zomboid's shipped `ProjectZomboid64.json` sets `-Xmx8g`. The compose
file sets `mem_limit: ${PROJECT_ZOMBOID_MEMORY_LIMIT:-8g}` - exactly the same
number. A JVM's resident set is heap PLUS metaspace, code cache, thread stacks,
direct byte buffers and GC control structures; PZ additionally loads native
Steam libraries (`steamclient.so` is 47 MB alone) and runs `-XX:+UseZGC`, which
carries higher native overhead than G1.

So the container limit is set to the heap size, guaranteeing that a heap which
actually grows to its configured maximum pushes total RSS past the cgroup limit.

## Evidence

Live container on this host:

```
$ docker exec <pz> cat /data/serverfiles/ProjectZomboid64.json
  "vmArgs": [ ..., "-Xmx8g", ..., "-XX:+UseZGC", ... ]

$ docker inspect --format '{{.HostConfig.Memory}}' <pz>
8589934592          # 8 GiB  == -Xmx8g exactly

$ docker exec <pz> grep MaxPlayers /data/Zomboid/Server/*.ini
MaxPlayers=16
```

The game's own documentation makes the heap the binding constraint, not system
RAM: pzwiki.net `Dedicated_Server` notes the shipped start script specifies
16 GB and warns "the server will fail to start with memory errors" if `-Xmx` is
not matched to available memory. Published sizing for ~10 players is roughly a
6 GB base plus ~0.5 GB per player (~11 GB heap); the repo provisions 8 GiB
total, heap included.

## Impact

The host runs cgroup v2 with swap accounting, and Docker set each container's
swap allowance equal to its memory limit:

```
$ cat /sys/fs/cgroup/.../<pz>/memory.max        # 8589934592  (8 GiB)
$ cat /sys/fs/cgroup/.../<pz>/memory.swap.max   # 8589934592  (8 GiB)
```

So the failure is staged, not instant:

1. Swap thrash (the failure that actually bites). Once RSS passes 8 GiB the
   kernel pages the JVM out to swap rather than killing it. For a latency-bound
   game loop this is worse than a clean crash: ZGC must touch swapped-out pages
   during collection, producing stalls of seconds to minutes while the server
   still appears "up" and healthy to Docker. `restart: unless-stopped` never
   triggers, and the container's healthcheck keeps reporting healthy.
2. OOM-kill, eventually. Only when heap + non-heap exceeds 16 GiB
   (memory.max + memory.swap.max) does the kernel SIGKILL the JVM. PZ writes
   player and chunk state continuously; a hard kill mid-write is the documented
   cause of corrupted `map_*.bin` chunk saves. `stop_grace_period: 3m` cannot
   help here - an OOM-kill is SIGKILL, not SIGTERM.
3. Under-provisioned for the stated target regardless. At 10 concurrent players
   the documented heap need (~11 GB) exceeds the entire 8 GiB container
   allocation, so the server enters state 1 well before reaching 10 users.

Note the stack-wide interaction: the four containers are collectively entitled
to 32 GiB of swap on a host with 31 GiB, so concurrent pressure oversubscribes
host swap too.

## Fix

Raise the container limit above the heap so the JVM has non-heap headroom, and
size the heap for 10 players. In `.env.example` and Coolify env:

```diff
-PROJECT_ZOMBOID_MEMORY_LIMIT=8g
+PROJECT_ZOMBOID_MEMORY_LIMIT=14g
```

and raise the heap to match the 10-player target:

```bash
./manage.sh exec project-zomboid sh -lc \
  'sed -i "s/-Xmx8g/-Xmx11g/" /data/serverfiles/ProjectZomboid64.json'
./manage.sh restart project-zomboid
```

11 GB heap inside a 14 GiB limit leaves ~3 GB for ZGC/native overhead. The
invariant to document and keep: `mem_limit` must always exceed `-Xmx` by a
meaningful margin - never equal it.

## Resolution
Raised -Xmx8g -> -Xmx11g in ProjectZomboid64.json and the container limit 8g -> 14g (docker update, and PROJECT_ZOMBOID_MEMORY_LIMIT=14g in .env.example/compose default). Verified live: PZ now sits at 9.03 GiB, which exceeds the old 8 GiB limit outright - confirming the finding was real. 14 GiB limit leaves ~3 GB non-heap headroom above the 11g heap.
title: Project Zomboid runs -Xmx8g inside an exactly-8GiB container, leaving zero headroom for JVM non-heap memory

body:
## Problem

`mem_limit: ${SEVEN_DAYS_TO_DIE_MEMORY_LIMIT:-10g}` is the largest allocation in
the stack, and it is still below the documented requirement for a 10-player
7 Days to Die server. 7DTD is a native Unity binary with no heap setting to tune
- the cgroup limit IS the hard ceiling, and breaching it is an immediate
SIGKILL with no GC backpressure and no graceful degradation.

## Evidence

Live container on this host:

```
$ docker inspect --format '{{.HostConfig.Memory}}' <sdtd>
10737418240         # 10 GiB

$ docker stats --no-stream
seven-days-to-die   2.007GiB / 10GiB   20.07%    # idle, zero players connected

$ docker exec <sdtd> grep GameWorld /data/serverfiles/sdtdserver.xml
<property name="GameWorld" value="Navezgane"/>
```

The 7D2D hosting wiki's "Server Hardware Requirements by Player Count" table
(wiki.7d2d.net/hosting/community/hardware-spec-guidance/) gives:

| Players | RAM |
| --- | --- |
| 4 - 8 players | 12 - 16 GB |
| 8 - 16 players | 16 - 32 GB |

10 players sits in the 8-16 tier: **16-32 GB**. The same page states the
allocation formula explicitly:

- "8 GB for game + 4 GB for OS = 12 GB minimum"
- "Player Scaling: Add 0.5 - 1 GB per additional player"

Applying the formula to the game process alone (excluding the 4 GB OS share,
since the OS lives outside this cgroup): 8 GB + (10 x 0.5-1 GB) = **13-18 GB**.
The provisioned 10 GiB is below the bottom of that range, and below even the
4-8 player tier's total.

Corroborating the sizing: the container already sits at 2.0 GiB with **zero**
players connected, so nearly the entire published per-player budget must come
out of the remaining 8 GiB.

## Impact

At ~10 concurrent players - especially during a blood moon horde, the game's
peak memory event, or with an 8K RWG map which the same doc says needs 2-4 GB
more than 6K - the container breaches its 10 GiB limit.

The host runs cgroup v2 and Docker gave the container a swap allowance equal to
its memory limit:

```
$ cat /sys/fs/cgroup/.../<sdtd>/memory.max        # 10737418240  (10 GiB)
$ cat /sys/fs/cgroup/.../<sdtd>/memory.swap.max   # 10737418240  (10 GiB)
```

so the server is first paged out to swap rather than killed. For a voxel
simulation this is the damaging outcome: tick rate collapses while the container
still reports healthy, `restart: unless-stopped` never fires, and players
experience rubber-banding and timeouts on horde night with nothing in the
container logs to explain it. Only past 20 GiB combined does the kernel SIGKILL
the process - and unlike a JVM there is no OutOfMemoryError and no chance to
flush, so 7DTD loses whatever region-file writes were in flight.

## Fix

Raise to the documented 8-16 player tier. In `.env.example` and Coolify env:

```diff
-SEVEN_DAYS_TO_DIE_MEMORY_LIMIT=10g
+SEVEN_DAYS_TO_DIE_MEMORY_LIMIT=16g
```

16g is the bottom of the documented 16-32 GB band and comfortably above the
13-18 GB the per-player formula yields. The host has 62 GiB total with ~50 GiB
available, so this fits alongside the other services.

## Resolution
Raised 10g -> 16g, the bottom of the documented 16-32 GB band for the 8-16 player tier. Applied live via docker update and set as the compose default / .env.example value. Verified: 2.005GiB / 16GiB.
title: 7 Days to Die is allocated 10g against a documented 16-32 GB requirement for its 8-16 player tier

body:
## Problem

Independent of memory sizing: the 7 Days to Die server is configured with
`ServerMaxPlayerCount=8`. Users 9 and 10 are refused at connection time. No
amount of `mem_limit` tuning changes this - the stated goal of "10 users" is
unreachable on this service as configured.

## Evidence

Live container on this host:

```
$ docker exec <sdtd> grep ServerMaxPlayerCount /data/serverfiles/sdtdserver.xml
<property name="ServerMaxPlayerCount"  value="8"/>   <!-- Maximum Concurrent Players -->
```

For contrast, the other three services do permit 10:

```
$ docker exec <mc> grep max-players /data/serverfiles/server.properties
max-players=20
$ docker exec <pz> grep MaxPlayers /data/Zomboid/Server/*.ini
MaxPlayers=16
```

(Valheim's vanilla cap is 10, i.e. exactly at target.)

## Impact

The 9th and 10th concurrent player receive a "server full" rejection. This is a
silent capacity ceiling: nothing in this repository documents the per-game player
cap, so an operator sizing memory for 10 users would reasonably assume 10 users
can connect, and would discover otherwise only when the group grows.

## Fix

Raise the cap to at least the target concurrency:

```bash
./manage.sh exec seven-days-to-die sh -lc \
  'sed -i "s/\"ServerMaxPlayerCount\"\(\s*\)value=\"8\"/\"ServerMaxPlayerCount\"\1value=\"10\"/" /data/serverfiles/sdtdserver.xml'
./manage.sh restart seven-days-to-die
```

Then verify with `./manage.sh exec seven-days-to-die grep ServerMaxPlayerCount
/data/serverfiles/sdtdserver.xml`. Note this must be paired with the memory
increase filed alongside it - raising the cap to 10 without raising `mem_limit`
converts a "server full" rejection into an OOM-kill.

Document the intended concurrency target and each game's player cap in the
README so the two settings stay reconciled.

## Resolution
ServerMaxPlayerCount 8 -> 10 in /data/serverfiles/sdtdserver.xml, restarted. Verified live: value="10". Paired with the memory increase to 16g so the raised cap cannot turn a 'server full' rejection into an OOM.
title: 7 Days to Die is configured to accept a maximum of 8 players, so it cannot host 10 users regardless of memory

body:
## Problem

The audit target is "enough memory for 10 users". Valheim's 6g limit is
adequate on paper, but the service is currently serving **zero** users: the game
process is not running at all and has been crash-looping for at least an hour.

LinuxGSM's `vhserver` requires `serverpassword` (minimum 5 characters). It is
empty, `monitor` fails on it, and the server exits shortly after each start.
Neither `docker-compose.yaml` nor `.env.example` exposes any variable to set it -
the only environment variable passed to the container is `TZ`.

## Evidence

Live container on this host, up 16h:

```
$ docker exec <vh> sh -lc 'ps -eo args | grep -c "[v]alheim_server.x86_64"'
0                                    # game process not running

$ docker stats --no-stream
valheim   45.58MiB / 6GiB   0.74%    # idle shell, not a running game

$ docker exec <vh> grep '^serverpassword' /data/config-lgsm/vhserver/_default.cfg
13:serverpassword="" # Minimum password length is 5.
```

LinuxGSM `monitor` states the cause outright:

```
$ ./manage.sh monitor valheim
[FAIL] Monitoring vhserver: serverpassword is not set
[ERROR] Monitoring vhserver: Checking session ... FAIL
[ OK ] Stopping vhserver / Starting vhserver: LinuxGSM
```

The restart loop is visible in the per-start script logs - 21 start attempts in
a single hour, roughly every 90 seconds:

```
$ docker exec <vh> sh -lc 'ls /data/log/script/vhserver-script-2026-07-30-17*.log | wc -l'
21
```

and the console log ends each cycle with the server tearing down:

```
17:30:45: Steam manager on destroy
17:30:45: ZNet OnDestroy
17:30:45: Net scene destroyed
```

`docker-compose.yaml:49-50` passes only `TZ`:

```yaml
    environment:
      TZ: ${TZ:-Europe/Helsinki}
```

## Impact

Valheim is completely unavailable - 0 of the 10 target users can connect, and
this has been true for the entire uptime of the deployment. It is invisible
through every channel this repo provides: `docker ps` shows "Up 16 hours
(healthy)", `restart: unless-stopped` never fires because the container never
exits, and `./manage.sh list` reports the container state, not the game state.

The 6g memory limit is therefore untested in practice; it cannot be validated
against a 10-player load until the server actually starts.

## Fix

Add a Valheim server password to the documented config surface. In
`.env.example`:

```diff
 # Valheim
+# Required: Valheim refuses to start without it. Minimum 5 characters.
+VALHEIM_SERVER_PASSWORD=changeme
 VALHEIM_MEMORY_LIMIT=6g
```

The LinuxGSM images do not template arbitrary settings from the environment, so
set it in the instance config that already exists in the volume:

```bash
./manage.sh exec valheim sh -lc \
  'echo "serverpassword=\"<at-least-5-chars>\"" >> /data/config-lgsm/vhserver/vhserver.cfg'
./manage.sh restart valheim
```

Then verify the server actually comes up, which is the check that was missing:

```bash
./manage.sh exec valheim sh -lc 'ps -eo args | grep -c "[v]alheim_server.x86_64"'   # expect >= 1
```

Note the password must not be identical to the server name (LinuxGSM/Valheim
reject that too). Filed separately: the healthcheck that reported this container
healthy throughout.

## Resolution
Set serverpassword in /data/config-lgsm/vhserver/vhserver.cfg (generated 20-char value, reported to the operator) and restarted. Verified live: valheim_server process now running, bound to 2457/udp, memory 1.087GiB (was 45MiB idle). Crash loop ended. VALHEIM_SERVER_PASSWORD added to .env.example as a placeholder and the requirement documented in README.
title: Valheim serves zero users: it is in a crash-restart loop because serverpassword is unset and the repo exposes no way to set it

body:
## Problem

Like Valheim, Project Zomboid is not serving anyone. The server starts, reaches
Project Zomboid's interactive "Enter new administrator password:" prompt, and
blocks there forever because nothing is attached to its stdin. It never binds
its game ports, so no player can connect.

LinuxGSM's `adminpassword` is still the shipped placeholder `CHANGE_ME`, and it
is not passed to the server on the command line - `startparameters` contains
only `-servername`.

## Evidence

Live container on this host:

```
$ docker exec <pz> sh -lc 'ps -eo pid,rss,args | grep "[P]rojectZomboid"'
1526569 351304 ./ProjectZomboid64 -servername pzserver     # ~343 MB RSS, alive but stalled
```

The console log ends at the prompt every time:

```
LOG : General ... version=42.20.0 a2947723ca demo=false
LOG : General ... SteamUtils initialised successfully
LOG : General ... Waiting for response from Steam servers
LOG : General ... User 'admin' not found, creating it
LOG : General ... Command line admin password: null
LOG : General ... Enter new administrator password:      <-- blocks here
```

The password is never supplied:

```
$ docker exec <pz> grep -n adminpassword /data/config-lgsm/pzserver/_default.cfg
13:adminpassword="CHANGE_ME"

$ docker exec <pz> grep -n startparameters /data/config-lgsm/pzserver/_default.cfg
16:startparameters="-servername ${selfname}"      # adminpassword not passed
```

Consequences visible from the host - the documented game ports are dead:

```
$ ss -lnu | grep -E ':(16261|16262)'
(no output)                                       # NOT LISTENING
```

and the in-container monitor keeps retrying:

```
$ docker exec <pz> sh -lc 'ls /data/log/script/pzserver-script-*.log | wc -l'
102                                               # 102 start attempts
```

For contrast, the two working services do bind:

```
$ ss -lnt | grep -E ':(25565|26900)'
tcp 0.0.0.0:26900   users:(("7DaysToDieServe",...))
tcp *:25565         users:(("java",...))
```

## Impact

0 of the 10 target users can connect to Project Zomboid, and this has been true
for the deployment's entire uptime. As with Valheim, every status surface this
repo offers reports green: the container is "Up 16 hours (healthy)",
`restart: unless-stopped` never fires, and `./manage.sh list` reports container
state rather than game state.

The memory finding filed against this service (`-Xmx8g` equal to an 8 GiB
`mem_limit`) remains valid and unverified in practice - it will bite as soon as
the server actually starts and accumulates players.

## Fix

Supply the admin password non-interactively so the prompt never appears. Set it
in the instance config and pass it through start parameters:

```bash
./manage.sh exec project-zomboid sh -lc \
  'printf "%s\n" "adminpassword=\"<strong-password>\"" >> /data/config-lgsm/pzserver/pzserver.cfg'
./manage.sh exec project-zomboid sh -lc \
  'printf "%s\n" "startparameters=\"-servername \${selfname} -adminpassword \${adminpassword}\"" >> /data/config-lgsm/pzserver/pzserver.cfg'
./manage.sh restart project-zomboid
```

Verify it actually came up - the check that was missing:

```bash
ss -lnu | grep -E ':(16261|16262)'    # expect the ports to be bound
```

Add `PROJECT_ZOMBOID_ADMIN_PASSWORD` to `.env.example` as a documented required
value with a placeholder (never a real secret), and note in README.md that both
Project Zomboid and Valheim require credentials before first start. Filed
separately: the healthcheck that reported this container healthy for 16 hours
while it was stalled.

## Resolution
Set adminpassword and appended '-adminpassword' to startparameters in /data/config-lgsm/pzserver/pzserver.cfg so the interactive prompt is never reached. Verified live: console reaches '*** SERVER STARTED ****', RCON on 27015, and the game ports 16261+16262/udp are bound. 102 start attempts stopped. PROJECT_ZOMBOID_ADMIN_PASSWORD added to .env.example as a placeholder. FOLLOW-UP: the password is visible in the process argv; now that the admin user exists it can be dropped from startparameters on a later restart.
title: Project Zomboid serves zero users: it blocks on an interactive admin-password prompt on every start, 102 attempts logged

body:
## Problem

The four services declare `cpus:` limits of 4 + 4 + 3 + 4 = 15 CPUs. The host
has 8. Memory limits are additive and enforced per-cgroup; CPU quota is too, so
the stack can request nearly twice the CPU the host owns.

## Evidence

```
$ nproc
8

$ for s in minecraft project-zomboid valheim seven-days-to-die; do \
    docker inspect --format '{{.HostConfig.NanoCpus}}' <$s>; done
4000000000   # 4.0 CPU
4000000000   # 4.0 CPU
3000000000   # 3.0 CPU
4000000000   # 4.0 CPU
                                 -----
                                 15.0 CPU on an 8-CPU host
```

By contrast the memory limits (8+8+6+10 = 32 GiB) fit inside the host's 62 GiB,
so memory is overcommitted only after the increases filed alongside this
(8+14+6+16 = 44 GiB, still within budget). CPU is the resource actually
oversubscribed.

## Impact

Under simultaneous load the kernel's CFS scheduler arbitrates, and every server
gets less CPU than its declared limit implies. This matters disproportionately
here because all four of these games are single-thread-bound on their main
simulation loop - the 7D2D hardware guidance states "7DTD's game logic runs
primarily on a single thread, making CPU clock speed the most critical factor".
The symptom is simultaneous tick-rate degradation across all four servers during
overlapping peak play, which is precisely when 10 concurrent users would be
present. The limits also give a false impression of headroom when capacity
planning.

## Fix

This is a deliberate-overcommit decision, not automatically a bug - it is
reasonable if the four games are never busy at once. Make the decision explicit
rather than accidental:

- If concurrent peak use is expected, size the limits to the host:
  e.g. 3 / 3 / 2 / 3 = 11, or drop to 2 / 2 / 2 / 2 = 8 for strict fit.
- If overcommit is intentional, record it in `.env.example` next to the
  `*_CPU_LIMIT` values ("sum intentionally exceeds host cores; games are not
  expected to peak simultaneously") so the next operator does not read 15 as
  available capacity.

Either way, document the host's core count as the sizing basis.

## Resolution
Reduced declared CPU from 4/4/3/4 (15) to 3/3/2/3 (11) on the 8-core host, applied live via docker update and set as compose defaults. The residual mild overcommit is now deliberate and documented in both .env.example and the README Sizing section.
title: Declared CPU limits total 15 cores on an 8-core host, a ~1.9x overcommit

body:
## Problem

`.env.example` lists eight resource knobs as bare values with no stated basis,
and README.md says only "adjust the resource limits for the host". Nothing
records what player count the numbers were sized for, nor - critically - that
for two of the four services the container limit is NOT the setting that bounds
the game's memory.

This is the systemic cause behind the per-service findings filed alongside it:
an operator turning `MINECRAFT_MEMORY_LIMIT` up to 8g reasonably believes they
gave Minecraft 8 GB, when LinuxGSM still runs it with `-Xmx1024M`.

## Evidence

`.env.example` in full, for the memory knobs:

```
# Minecraft (Java Edition)
MINECRAFT_MEMORY_LIMIT=8g
...
# 7 Days to Die
SEVEN_DAYS_TO_DIE_MEMORY_LIMIT=10g
```

README.md:1-20 documents deployment and says "Copy `.env.example` values to
Coolify's environment variables and adjust the resource limits for the host."
There is no sizing table, no target player count, and no mention of `javaram`
(Minecraft), `-Xmx` in `ProjectZomboid64.json` (Project Zomboid),
`ServerMaxPlayerCount` (7 Days to Die), or `MaxPlayers`/`max-players`.

Confirmed drift between the documented knob and the effective one:

```
MINECRAFT_MEMORY_LIMIT=8g   ->  actual heap: java -Xmx1024M   (12.5% of it)
```

## Impact

The documented config surface is misleading for the exact operation an operator
performs when scaling to more users. Two of the four services silently ignore
the knob the repo tells them to turn (Minecraft entirely; Project Zomboid's heap
is set inside the volume, not by this variable). Player caps are undocumented,
so 7DTD's 8-player ceiling is invisible until users are turned away.

## Fix

Add a sizing table to README.md stating the target concurrency and, per service,
both the container limit and the in-game/in-runtime setting that actually bounds
memory and players:

| Server | Container limit | Game memory setting | Player cap setting |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Minecraft | `MINECRAFT_MEMORY_LIMIT` | `javaram` in `/data/config-lgsm/mcserver/mcserver.cfg` | `max-players` in `server.properties` |
| Project Zomboid | `PROJECT_ZOMBOID_MEMORY_LIMIT` | `-Xmx` in `/data/serverfiles/ProjectZomboid64.json` | `MaxPlayers` in the server `.ini` |
| Valheim | `VALHEIM_MEMORY_LIMIT` | none (native) | vanilla cap 10 |
| 7 Days to Die | `SEVEN_DAYS_TO_DIE_MEMORY_LIMIT` | none (native) | `ServerMaxPlayerCount` in `sdtdserver.xml` |

Add a comment header to `.env.example` recording the sizing target
("sized for 10 concurrent players; see README sizing table") and the invariant
that for JVM servers `mem_limit` must exceed `-Xmx`.

## Resolution
Added a Sizing table to README.md giving, per service, the container limit, the game's own memory setting, the player-cap setting, and the documented 10-player basis. .env.example now carries a header stating the 10-player target and the invariant that mem_limit must exceed the game heap, plus per-service comments.
title: Memory and CPU limits are documented as bare numbers with no player-count basis and no warning that mem_limit is not the game's heap

body:
## Problem

Three functions hardcode `docker exec -it`. The `-i` flag attaches stdin, and
Docker refuses when stdin is not a terminal. Every command routed through them
therefore fails outright under cron, CI, `nohup`, a pipe, or any non-interactive
shell - the exact contexts in which an operations script is most useful.

`console` and `shell` genuinely need a TTY. `details` and `exec` do not: they
run a command and print its output.

## Evidence

```
manage.sh:180  docker exec -it --user "$LINUXGSM_USER" "$id" "./$script" "$command"   # run_lgsm
manage.sh:260  docker exec -it --user "$LINUXGSM_USER" "$id" "$shell"                 # open_shell
manage.sh:269  docker exec -it --user "$LINUXGSM_USER" "$id" "$@"                     # exec_in_container
```

Reproduced against the live stack, stdin redirected from `/dev/null` to simulate
cron:

```
$ ./manage.sh exec valheim echo hello </dev/null; echo "exit=$?"
cannot attach stdin to a TTY-enabled container because stdin is not a terminal
exit=1

$ ./manage.sh details valheim </dev/null; echo "exit=$?"
[INFO] Valheim: ./vhserver details (valheim-...)
cannot attach stdin to a TTY-enabled container because stdin is not a terminal
exit=1
```

`details` is dispatched through `run_lgsm` (`manage.sh:397`), which is the
`-it` path. The sibling `run_lgsm_noninteractive` already exists and omits
`-it` - `monitor` works fine non-interactively for exactly that reason.

README.md:35-42 recommends `details` as the way to verify effective ports, and
README.md:70-72 recommends driving `manage.sh` from crontab. Anyone scripting
around the documented `details` invocation gets exit 1.

## Impact

`exec` and `details` cannot be used from cron, CI, or any wrapper script; they
fail with a Docker-level error that does not name the real cause. The failure is
silent-by-confusion rather than silent - the message blames stdin, not the
script's flag choice.

## Fix

Allocate a TTY only when there is one. Add a helper and use it in the three call
sites:

```bash
tty_flags() {
  if [[ -t 0 && -t 1 ]]; then printf '%s\n' -i -t; fi
}
```

then:

```bash
# run_lgsm
mapfile -t tty < <(tty_flags)
docker exec "${tty[@]}" --user "$LINUXGSM_USER" "$id" "./$script" "$command"
```

Apply the same in `exec_in_container`. Leave `open_shell` and `console`
requiring a TTY, but fail fast with a clear message instead of Docker's:

```bash
[[ -t 0 ]] || die "'shell' requires an interactive terminal."
```

Add a bats case asserting `exec` succeeds with stdin redirected from
`/dev/null`; the current suite never exercises the non-TTY path.

## Resolution
Replaced the three hardcoded 'docker exec -it' call sites with a docker_exec_tty helper that adds -i -t only when both stdin and stdout are terminals; console and shell now fail fast via require_tty with a clear message instead of Docker's. Verified: './manage.sh exec valheim echo hello </dev/null' now exits 0 and prints hello (was exit 1). Two bats cases added covering the non-TTY exec path and the shell fail-fast path.
title: docker exec -it makes exec, details, console and shell fail with exit 1 whenever stdin is not a TTY

body:
## Problem

The LinuxGSM image's healthcheck runs `monitor`, and LinuxGSM `monitor`'s
behaviour on a dead server is to **restart it and exit 0**. A server that dies
on every start therefore reports `healthy` forever. Nothing in the compose file
overrides this.

This is not theoretical: the Valheim service has been crash-looping for the
entire deployment while Docker reported it healthy with a failing streak of
zero.

## Evidence

The image's healthcheck and its implementation:

```
$ docker inspect --format '{{json .Config.Healthcheck}}' <vh>
{"Test":["CMD-SHELL","/app/entrypoint-healthcheck.sh || exit 1"],
 "Interval":60000000000,"Timeout":60000000000,"StartPeriod":120000000000,"Retries":1}

$ docker exec <vh> cat /app/entrypoint-healthcheck.sh
#!/bin/bash
exec gosu "${USER}" /app/*server monitor || exit 1
```

`monitor` restarts a dead server, so it succeeds precisely when the server was
broken. Observed simultaneously on the live host:

```
$ docker exec <vh> sh -lc 'ps -eo args | grep -c "[v]alheim_server.x86_64"'
0                                              # game process dead

$ docker inspect --format 'Health={{.State.Health.Status}} FailingStreak={{.State.Health.FailingStreak}}' <vh>
Health=healthy FailingStreak=0                 # reported healthy anyway

$ docker exec <vh> sh -lc 'ls /data/log/script/vhserver-script-2026-07-30-17*.log | wc -l'
21                                             # 21 restarts in one hour
```

`manage.sh`'s own `list` does not close the gap either. `print_list`
(manage.sh:226-231) derives `LINUXGSM` state from `./$script details` exiting 0,
which also succeeds for a stopped-but-installed server, and `doctor`
(manage.sh:304-318) checks only `container_state == running`.

## Impact

The stack has no signal that distinguishes "server up" from "server restarting
every 90 seconds". Every monitoring surface available - `docker ps`, Coolify's
health column, `./manage.sh list`, `./manage.sh doctor` - showed green for a
service serving zero players for 16 hours. An operator has no reason to look,
which is why the Valheim outage persisted.

## Fix

Two cheap changes; neither needs new tooling.

1. Report actual game-process state in `list` and `doctor` rather than only
   container state. LinuxGSM already tracks this - the session check is what
   `monitor` uses. Add to `print_list`, replacing the `details`-exit-code probe:

   ```bash
   if docker exec --user "$LINUXGSM_USER" "$id" \
        sh -lc 'pgrep -f "[s]erver.x86_64|minecraft_server.jar|ProjectZomboid" >/dev/null'; then
     lgsm_state="running"
   else
     lgsm_state="DOWN"
   fi
   ```

2. Make the crash loop visible by counting recent starts in `doctor`, which is
   the command whose job is exactly this:

   ```bash
   starts=$(docker exec --user "$LINUXGSM_USER" "$id" \
     sh -lc 'ls /data/log/script/*-script-*.log 2>/dev/null | wc -l')
   (( starts < 5 )) || log_warn "${DISPLAY_NAMES[$service]}: $starts start attempts logged - possible restart loop"
   ```

Optionally disable the self-healing healthcheck in `docker-compose.yaml` so
Docker's health reflects state rather than performing repair:

```yaml
    healthcheck:
      test: ["CMD-SHELL", "pgrep -f 'server.x86_64|minecraft_server.jar' >/dev/null || exit 1"]
      interval: 60s
      retries: 3
```

## Resolution
Three changes: (1) docker-compose.yaml now overrides the image healthcheck with a per-service pgrep on the actual game binary, replacing the LinuxGSM 'monitor' default that repaired-and-exited-0 and could never report unhealthy; (2) manage.sh list now reports game-process state (running/DOWN) instead of a details-exit-code probe; (3) doctor now fails when the container is up but the game is dead, and warns on repeated LinuxGSM start attempts in the last hour. Verified: doctor correctly reported both outages before the fixes and reports all four healthy after. NOTE: the compose healthcheck takes effect only on the next Coolify redeploy.
title: Container health can never report unhealthy for a crash-looping server, because the healthcheck action is to restart it

body:
## Problem

The repository has no CI/CD definition of any kind - no `.github/`, no
`.gitlab-ci.yml`, no pipeline file. It nonetheless ships a test suite and code
that is clean under three linters. Every one of those checks is opt-in and
manual, so a regression is caught only if a human remembers to run them.

## Evidence

```
$ ls -la /home/ivuorinen/Code/eslefi/gs
docker-compose.yaml  docs/  .env.example  LICENSE  manage.sh  README.md  test/
$ ls .github
ls: cannot access '.github': No such file or directory
```

All four checks currently pass and are therefore cheap to gate:

```
$ shellcheck -x manage.sh          ; echo $?   -> 0
$ yamllint docker-compose.yaml     ; echo $?   -> 0
$ docker compose config -q         ; echo $?   -> 0
$ bats test/manage.bats
1..8
ok 1 restart on a missing container prints exactly one diagnostic and exits 1
...
ok 8 an unknown command is rejected                        -> 0
```

The store's own history records why this matters: `NP-001` and the
`upgrade_one` finding were both error-propagation regressions in `manage.sh`,
and the bats suite exists specifically to catch their recurrence. Ungated, it
catches nothing automatically.

## Impact

The regression suite written in response to two real correctness bugs does not
run on push or pull request. A change reintroducing either bug merges green.

## Fix

Add `.github/workflows/ci.yml`. `bats` runs without a daemon because the suite
stubs `docker` via PATH injection, so no services are needed:

```yaml
name: ci
on:
  push:
  pull_request:
permissions:
  contents: read
jobs:
  check:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - run: sudo apt-get update && sudo apt-get install -y shellcheck bats yamllint
      - run: shellcheck -x manage.sh test/manage.bats
      - run: yamllint docker-compose.yaml
      - run: docker compose config -q
      - run: bats test/manage.bats
```

Pin `actions/checkout` by commit SHA if third-party action pinning is a policy
here; `actions/*` by major tag is the common baseline.

## Resolution
Added .github/workflows/ci.yml running shellcheck, yamllint, docker compose config -q, and bats on push and pull_request, plus a guard that fails the build on shfmt-corrupted associative array keys. All steps pass locally.
title: The repo ships a passing bats suite and lints clean, but nothing gates either on push or PR

body:
## Problem

README.md tells operators to "Open at least the following default ports on the
host and any upstream firewall" and then gives a table. Checked against what the
running servers actually bind on this host, the table is missing two ports.

## Evidence

README.md:28-33 documents:

| Server | Ports |
| --- | --- |
| Minecraft | `25565/tcp` |
| Project Zomboid | `16261/udp`, player ports beginning at `16262/udp` |
| Valheim | `2456-2458/udp` |
| 7 Days to Die | `26900/tcp`, `26900-26903/udp` |

Actually bound (`ss -lntup`, host networking so these are host ports):

```
tcp *:25565          users:(("java",...))              # documented
udp *:25565          users:(("java",...))              # NOT documented
tcp 0.0.0.0:26900    users:(("7DaysToDieServe",...))   # documented
udp 0.0.0.0:26900    users:(("7DaysToDieServe",...))   # documented
udp 0.0.0.0:26902    users:(("7DaysToDieServe",...))   # documented
udp 0.0.0.0:11000    users:(("7DaysToDieServe",...))   # NOT documented
udp 0.0.0.0:50425    users:(("7DaysToDieServe",...))   # ephemeral Steam, not documented
udp 0.0.0.0:56830    users:(("7DaysToDieServe",...))   # ephemeral Steam, not documented
```

Minecraft's UDP 25565 is the query listener, and it is enabled in config:

```
$ docker exec <mc> grep -E "^enable-query|^query.port" /data/serverfiles/server.properties
enable-query=true
query.port=25565
```

7 Days to Die's UDP 11000 is its Steam networking port, outside the documented
26900-26903 range.

Project Zomboid's and Valheim's rows could not be verified against reality
because neither server is currently running (filed separately) - their
documented ports match their config files (`DefaultPort=16261`,
`UDPPort=16262`, `port="2456"`), but nothing is bound to confirm.

## Impact

An operator who opens exactly what the table lists gets a Minecraft server that
is unreachable by server-list query/ping (players see it as offline in the
multiplayer list even though it accepts direct connections), and a 7 Days to Die
server whose Steam networking path is blocked. Both present as "the server
doesn't show up" with no error anywhere, which is expensive to diagnose.

## Fix

Correct the table to match what the servers bind:

```diff
 | Server | Ports |
 | --- | --- |
-| Minecraft | `25565/tcp` |
+| Minecraft | `25565/tcp`, `25565/udp` (query; `enable-query=true`) |
 | Project Zomboid | `16261/udp`, player ports beginning at `16262/udp` |
 | Valheim | `2456-2458/udp` |
-| 7 Days to Die | `26900/tcp`, `26900-26903/udp` |
+| 7 Days to Die | `26900/tcp`, `26900-26903/udp`, `11000/udp` (Steam networking) |
```

The README already tells operators to "Verify the effective ports after
installation" with `./manage.sh details <server>` - note that `doctor` already
runs `port_summary` (`manage.sh:279-283`) and is the better check, since it
reads actual listeners rather than configured values.

## Resolution
Corrected the README firewall table: added Minecraft 25565/udp (query, enable-query=true) and 7 Days to Die 11000/udp (Steam networking), both verified bound via ss. Added a note that omitting Minecraft's UDP port hides the server from the multiplayer list.
title: The firewall table omits ports the servers actually bind: Minecraft 25565/udp and 7 Days to Die 11000/udp

body:
## Problem

The suite is genuinely useful - all 8 tests pass and they pin the two
error-propagation regressions the store records as previously fixed. But its
coverage is narrow: it exercises command dispatch and missing-container handling
and nothing else. Several commands with real branching have zero tests.

## Evidence

```
$ bats test/manage.bats
1..8   ... all pass
```

The 8 tests cover: `restart` (single/all/missing), `upgrade` (single/all),
`list` with a missing container, unknown server, unknown command.

Untested surfaces with non-trivial logic:

- `doctor` (manage.sh:285-328) - accumulates `failures`, branches on docker
  availability, container state, and `ss` presence, and its return code is the
  script's exit code. No test.
- `show_logs` (manage.sh:246-254) - the `--follow`/`-f` argument parsing at
  manage.sh:409 uses a nested command substitution that is easy to break. No test.
- `container_id` multi-container branch (manage.sh:127-133) - warns and picks
  the newest; the mock never returns two IDs, so this path has never run.
- `print_list` state column (manage.sh:226-231) - the `lgsm_state`
  available/check-failed branch. Only the "missing" row is asserted.
- Non-TTY invocation - `exec` and `details` fail with exit 1 when stdin is not a
  terminal (filed separately as `audit-290ecaba`). The mock `docker` ignores
  `-it` entirely, so the suite cannot catch it.

The mock (test/manage.bats:20-71) also always reports `State.Status` as
`running`, so `require_running_container`'s "not running" die path
(manage.sh:168) is never exercised.

## Impact

The regressions the suite was written for are pinned, but adjacent logic in the
same file is not. `doctor` in particular is the command an operator reaches for
when something is wrong, and its failure-counting is unverified.

## Fix

Add cases using the existing mock harness - no new tooling, the PATH-injection
pattern already supports all of these:

```bash
@test "doctor exits 1 when a container is missing" {
  export MOCK_MISSING_SERVICE=valheim
  run bash "$MANAGE_SH" doctor
  [ "$status" -eq 1 ]
  [[ "$output" == *"Valheim: container missing"* ]]
}

@test "doctor exits 0 when every container is running" {
  run bash "$MANAGE_SH" doctor
  [ "$status" -eq 0 ]
}

@test "logs --follow passes --follow to docker" {
  run bash "$MANAGE_SH" logs minecraft --follow
  [[ "$output" == *"--follow"* ]]
}

@test "exec works when stdin is not a TTY" {
  run bash -c "bash '$MANAGE_SH' exec valheim echo hello </dev/null"
  [ "$status" -eq 0 ]
}
```

The `logs` case needs a `logs` branch in the mock `docker` (it currently exits 1
on unhandled subcommands), and a `MOCK_STOPPED_SERVICE` variable would let the
mock report a non-running state so the stopped-container path can be covered.

## Resolution
Suite grown from 8 to 16 tests. Added: doctor exit 1 on missing container, doctor exit 0 when healthy, logs --follow passthrough (both directions), exec on a non-TTY stdin, exec with no command, shell fail-fast without a TTY, and 'all' rejection for single-server commands. Mock docker extended with a logs branch and flag-skipping in the exec branch. All 16 pass; shellcheck clean.
title: The bats suite covers only the container-lookup error paths; doctor, logs, list formatting and the non-TTY path are untested

body:
## Problem

`shfmt` misparses hyphenated associative-array keys as arithmetic subtraction
and rewrites them with spaces. Since the repo has no formatter config and no CI,
anyone who runs `shfmt -w manage.sh` - a routine thing to do on a shell repo -
silently breaks the script.

## Evidence

```
$ shfmt -d -i 2 -ci manage.sh
--- manage.sh.orig
+++ manage.sh
@@ -16,17 +16,17 @@
 declare -A DISPLAY_NAMES=(
   [minecraft]="Minecraft"
-  [project-zomboid]="Project Zomboid"
+  [project - zomboid]="Project Zomboid"
   [valheim]="Valheim"
-  [seven-days-to-die]="7 Days to Die"
+  [seven - days - to - die]="7 Days to Die"
 )
```

The same corruption is applied to `DEFAULT_SCRIPTS`. After such a write,
`${DISPLAY_NAMES[$service]}` and `${DEFAULT_SCRIPTS[$service]}` miss for three of
the four services, so every command against `project-zomboid`,
`seven-days-to-die`, and their `all` iterations breaks.

This is the same class of shellcheck/shfmt parser limitation already recorded in
the resolved ledger as `NP-003` (`readonly -A` triggering 8 false SC2154
warnings), fixed there by splitting `declare -A` from `readonly`. shellcheck is
now clean; shfmt is not.

## Impact

A formatting pass - the least suspicious kind of commit - produces a broken
script with no error at write time. The existing bats suite would catch it
(tests 2, 3 and 5 assert the display names), but only if someone runs it, and
nothing does automatically.

## Fix

Two options, both cheap; take the first.

1. Exclude the file from shfmt via an `.editorconfig` at the repo root, which
   shfmt reads natively:

   ```ini
   [manage.sh]
   shell_variant = bash
   ```

   and record the hazard in a comment above the arrays:

   ```bash
   # shfmt misparses hyphenated assoc-array keys ([a-b] as arithmetic); do not
   # run `shfmt -w` on this file. See docs/audit findings.
   ```

2. Or sidestep the parser entirely by assigning keys individually, which shfmt
   handles correctly:

   ```bash
   declare -A DISPLAY_NAMES=()
   DISPLAY_NAMES[minecraft]="Minecraft"
   DISPLAY_NAMES[project-zomboid]="Project Zomboid"
   ```

Either way, the CI workflow filed under `ci-88c92ca1` should run `bats` so a
corrupting format pass fails the build.

## Resolution
Added a comment above the associative arrays warning against shfmt -w and explaining the corruption, plus a CI step that greps for the mangled '[project - ' / '[seven - ' form and fails the build. Chose the guard over an .editorconfig because CI enforcement catches it regardless of local tooling.
title: Running shfmt -w on manage.sh silently corrupts the associative array keys

body:
## Problem

`.env`/`.env.example` never set `PROJECT_ZOMBOID_INI_Public` or
`PROJECT_ZOMBOID_INI_PublicName`, so `pzserver.ini` kept the PZ defaults
`Public=false` and `PublicName=LinuxGSM`. Every other player-facing PZ setting
(MaxPlayers, Password) was pushed through `apply-config`; discoverability was
not, so the server was invisible to the in-game browser and tagged `hidden` in
its Steam query reply.

## Evidence

Before the fix, A2S_RULES against 127.0.0.1:16261 returned
`open=1, public=0, pvp=1, version=42.20` and A2S_INFO carried the keyword
string `hidden;vanilla;pvp;` under the name `LinuxGSM`.
`/data/Zomboid/Server/pzserver.ini:78` read `Public=false`, `:81`
`PublicName=LinuxGSM`. `/data/Zomboid/Logs/` contained no user log file at all —
no player had ever completed a login since the 2026-07-29 install.

## Impact

A player who located the server anyway (favourite/direct IP) hung on
"Getting server info" and could not join. Reported by a user 2026-08-01.

## Fix

Set in `.env` and `.env.example`:
`PROJECT_ZOMBOID_INI_Public=true` and `PROJECT_ZOMBOID_INI_PublicName=<name>`,
then `./manage.sh apply-config project-zomboid && ./manage.sh restart project-zomboid`.

## Resolution
Set PROJECT_ZOMBOID_INI_Public=true and PublicName in .env/.env.example; applied and restarted. A2S_RULES now reports public=1, the 'hidden' keyword is gone and the server advertises as 'eslefi'.
title: Project Zomboid was never advertised: Public defaults to false

body:
## Problem

The Project Zomboid server starts with `*** Steam is enabled` but its Steam API
never initialises, so it never registers a Steam game server. The legacy A2S
responder still answers, which masks the failure from every health check in the
repo (`docker-compose.yaml` pgreps the process; `manage.sh doctor` checks the
same).

## Evidence

`/data/log/console/pzserver-console.log`, every boot including after the
2026-08-01 restart:

    [S_API] SteamAPI_Init(): Loaded local 'steamclient.so' OK.
    SteamInternal_SetMinidumpSteamID: Caching Steam ID: 76561197960265728 [API loaded no]
    LOG : General > Waiting for response from Steam servers
    [S_API FAIL] Tried to access Steam interface SteamNetworkingUtils004 before SteamAPI_Init succeeded.
    LOG : Network > *** SERVER STARTED ****
    LOG : Network > *** Steam is enabled

The decoded A2S_INFO reply reports AppID 0 rather than 108600. From the
first boot onward the log fills with paired `STEAMPS3 - AsyncTCPSocket created`
/ `destroyed` lines - 4095 of them in 9 hours, one reconnect cycle every ~16 s,
which is a Steam CM connection that never establishes. Outbound reachability is
not the cause: from inside the container, TCP 27017/27019/443 to a Steam CM
connect successfully and `api.steampowered.com` resolves and responds.

## Impact

The server never appears in the Steam server list and cannot be reached over
Steam networking; only direct-IP joins against RakNet on UDP 16262 can work.
Any client path that resolves server info through Steam stalls indefinitely.

## Fix

Not yet diagnosed to root cause. Next step is to run the server with
`SteamVAC=false` to confirm the Steam layer is the blocker, and to check whether
the LinuxGSM `pz` image ships a `steam_appid.txt` containing 108600 next to
`ProjectZomboid64`; PZ's `SteamAPI_Init` fails silently without it. If Steam is
not wanted at all, disable it explicitly rather than leaving it enabled and
broken.

## Resolution
Finding was wrong. Steam Web API ISteamApps/GetServersAtAddress for 95.216.7.112 lists the server as appid=108600, gamedir=zomboid, gameport=16261, secure=true -- it IS registered with the Steam master server. The '[API loaded no]' and '[S_API FAIL] SteamNetworkingUtils004' lines refer to the Steam CLIENT API, which a dedicated server legitimately never initialises; the game-server API is up. steam_appid.txt exists with 108600. The AppID 0 in the A2S_INFO reply is what PZ writes in that field, not evidence of a failed registration, and the AsyncTCPSocket create/destroy pairs are log noise. Confirmed by tcpdump: Steam master-list scrapers from 8 distinct external IPs queried udp/16261 within seconds of Public=true, which only happens for a registered server.
title: Project Zomboid Steam API never initialises; server registers with AppID 0

body:
## Problem

`PROJECT_ZOMBOID_LGSM_STARTPARAMETERS` carries `-adminpassword <secret>`, which
puts the Project Zomboid admin password on the server's argv. The value is also
duplicated between `PROJECT_ZOMBOID_LGSM_ADMINPASSWORD` and the start-parameter
string, so the two can silently drift apart.

## Evidence

`ps -eo args` on the host, run as an unprivileged user, returns:

    ./ProjectZomboid64 -servername pzserver -adminpassword <secret>

The same value is written in clear text into
`/data/config-lgsm/pzserver/pzserver.cfg` inside the managed block, and appears
twice in `.env` and twice in `.env.example`.

## Impact

Every local user and every container able to read the host `/proc` can read the
Project Zomboid admin password. `network_mode: host` means the game containers
already share the host network namespace, widening who is in that blast radius.

## Fix

`-adminpassword` is only needed for the very first start, to keep the server off
its interactive "Enter new administrator password:" prompt; the password is
persisted in the server database afterwards. Once the server has started once,
drop `-adminpassword` from `PROJECT_ZOMBOID_LGSM_STARTPARAMETERS`, leaving
`PROJECT_ZOMBOID_LGSM_ADMINPASSWORD` as the single source, and note in
`.env.example` that the parameter is a first-boot-only bootstrap.

## Resolution
Dropped -adminpassword from PROJECT_ZOMBOID_LGSM_STARTPARAMETERS in .env (now '-servername pzserver'); .env.example keeps it but documents it as a first-boot-only bootstrap to remove after the first successful start. Safe because the account is persisted: pzserver.db whitelist has username 'admin', role 'admin', 60-char bcrypt hash. Verified after restart: ps -eo args shows './ProjectZomboid64 -servername pzserver', the server reached '*** SERVER STARTED ****' in 60s and the console log has 0 occurrences of 'Enter new administrator password'.
title: Project Zomboid admin password is exposed in the host process table

body:
## Problem

`apply_kv_config` and `apply_xml_config` built the in-container edit command by
interpolating the setting's value into the command *text*:

    docker exec ... sh -lc "f='$path'; k='$real'; v='$value'; ..."

Any value containing an apostrophe closed the `v='...'` quote early. The value
was then also handed to `sed` as a replacement string, where `|`, `&` and `\`
are metacharacters, and to a `sh -lc` where `$` and backticks are live.

## Evidence

Running the exact construct against a live container with
`value=drifter9000's Project Zomboid server`:

    $ docker exec --user linuxgsm <pz> sh -lc "f='/tmp/probe.ini'; k='PublicName'; \
        v='drifter9000's Project Zomboid server'; ..."
    sh: 1: Syntax error: Unterminated quoted string
    $ cat /tmp/probe.ini
    PublicName=old          <-- unchanged

The setting is dropped and the run continues; the only trace is a
`could not set 'PublicName' in pzserver.ini` warning, and `apply-config`
still exits 0. Every `<SERVICE>_PROP_`, `<SERVICE>_INI_` and
`<SERVICE>_XML_` setting was affected — that is Minecraft's MOTD, Project
Zomboid's PublicName/PublicDescription/ServerWelcomeMessage and 7 Days to
Die's ServerName/ServerDescription, i.e. exactly the free-text fields most
likely to contain an apostrophe.

## Impact

Server names and descriptions could not contain an apostrophe. A `&` or `|`
in a value would have been eaten by `sed` and silently corrupted the written
line rather than failing. Values reaching a shell inside the container is also
a command-execution path from a config file.

## Fix

Fetch the file, rewrite it host-side in bash, write the body back through a
pipe; the path travels as a `sh -c` positional argument and the value never
enters any command text or regex replacement. Added `xml_escape` so `&`/`<`
in a 7DTD value cannot produce XML the server refuses to parse. Covered by
`test/manage.bats`: "apply-config applies values containing apostrophes and
shell metacharacters".

## Resolution
apply_kv_config and apply_xml_config now fetch the file with read_remote_file, rewrite it host-side in bash and write it back with write_remote_file; the path travels as a sh -c positional argument and the value never enters command text or a sed replacement. Added xml_escape for &/</>/" in 7DTD values. Verified live: apply-config all wrote motd=drifter9000's Minecraft server, PublicName=drifter9000's Project Zomboid server, servername="drifter9000's Valheim server" and ServerName=drifter9000's 7 Days to Die server with zero warnings; sdtdserver.xml still parses (xml.dom.minidom) and line counts are unchanged (server.properties 79, pzserver.ini 421, sdtdserver.xml 108). shellcheck clean, bats 28/28 including the new apostrophe/metacharacter regression test.
title: apply-config spliced config values into a remote shell command, silently dropping any value with an apostrophe

body:
## Problem

`.env` opened its Tier 1 section with "Sized for 10 concurrent players" while
`.env.example` said 15 and every limit had been raised to 15.

## Evidence

Commit 5c14df6 ("feat: raise capacity to 15 players and add join passwords")
set `MINECRAFT_PROP_max_players=15`, `PROJECT_ZOMBOID_INI_MaxPlayers=15` and
`SEVEN_DAYS_TO_DIE_XML_ServerMaxPlayerCount=15`, and `.env.example:44` reads
"Sized for 15 concurrent players per server (Valheim: 10, see below)". The
`.env` header was not updated with them.

## Impact

The comment misstates the basis for the memory and CPU limits directly below
it, which is the one thing a reader consults before changing them.

## Fix

Restate as 15 per server, noting Valheim's vanilla cap of 10.

## Resolution
Tier 1 header in .env now reads 'Sized for 15 concurrent players per server (Valheim: 10 - vanilla is hard-capped there)', matching .env.example and the limits below it.
title: .env's Tier 1 header still claimed 10-player sizing after the raise to 15
